question_interpretation: Asks what Part 11 covers (scope) and which records it applies to — i.e., 11.1 and 11.2, including the records that are excluded.

issues.detail: J omits the express exclusions in 11.1: Part 11 does not apply to paper records transmitted by electronic means (11.1(b)), and does not apply to records required by Part 1 subparts J, L, M, O and R, parts 112, 117, 121 and 507, and to e-signatures under 101.11(d)/101.8(d) (11.1(f)-(p)), unless those records are also required under other provisions. The question asks 'to which records does it apply', so the exclusions are part of the answer.

J omits that Part 11 also applies to electronic records submitted to FDA under the FD&C Act and PHS Act even if not specifically identified in agency regulations (11.1(b), second sentence), and the 11.1(a) purpose (criteria for trustworthiness and equivalence) and 11.1(e) inspection availability of systems.
'Predicate rules' is guidance terminology; the regulation says 'under any records requirements set forth in agency regulations'. Acceptable shorthand.

explanation: 11.1 and 11.2 are the right sections and J's core element (electronic records created, modified, maintained, archived, retrieved or transmitted under agency records requirements; e-signatures; use in lieu of paper per 11.2) is supported. But J leaves out the coverage of records submitted to FDA and the exclusions in 11.1(b) and 11.1(f)-(p), which directly answer 'to which records does it apply'.
proposed_corrected_answer: Part 11 sets the criteria under which FDA considers electronic records and electronic signatures (and handwritten signatures executed to electronic records) trustworthy, reliable and generally equivalent to paper records and handwritten signatures (11.1(a)). It applies to records in electronic form that are created, modified, maintained, archived, retrieved or transmitted under any records requirement in FDA regulations (predicate rules), and to electronic records submitted to FDA under the FD&C Act or PHS Act even if not specifically identified in regulations (11.1(b)). It does not apply to paper records that are transmitted electronically (11.1(b)), and it excludes records required solely by Part 1 subparts J, L, M, O and R and by parts 112, 117, 121 and 507, plus e-signatures under 101.11(d) and 101.8(d) (11.1(f)-(p)); such records remain subject to Part 11 if also required under other provisions. Compliant e-signatures are treated as equivalent to handwritten signatures (11.1(c)); compliant electronic records may be used in lieu of paper per 11.2 unless paper is specifically required (11.1(d)); for submissions, the document type must be listed in public docket 92S-0251 (11.2(b)). Systems, controls and documentation must be available for FDA inspection (11.1(e)).

evidence.quote: This part applies to records in electronic form that are created, modified, maintained, archived, retrieved, or transmitted, under any records requirements set forth in agency regulations. This part also applies to electronic records submitted to the agency under requirements of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and the Public Health Service Act, even if such records are not specifically identified in agency regulations. However, this part does not apply to paper records that are, or have been, transmitted by electronic means.

question_interpretation: A regulated firm uses a cloud-hosted LIMS. Asks which Part 11 provisions apply to the vendor-hosted controls and how FDA's 2003 Scope and Application guidance affects enforcement discretion.

issues.detail: J lists enforcement discretion on 'validation, audit trails, legacy systems, and record copies' but omits record retention. The guidance names validation, audit trail, record retention and record copying, plus all Part 11 requirements for qualifying legacy systems.

J does not answer the 'vendor's controls' part. Part 11 obligations fall on the persons who use the system to create, modify, maintain or transmit records (11.10/11.30 introductory text), i.e., the regulated firm, not the vendor. Whether 11.10 (closed) or 11.30 (open) applies depends on whether system access is controlled by the persons responsible for the record content (11.3(b)(4), (b)(9)). The 2003 guidance does not address vendors or hosting.

J omits that FDA still enforces the other Part 11 provisions: 11.10 access limits, operational/authority/device checks, training, accountability policies and documentation controls; 11.30; and the signature requirements in 11.50, 11.70, 11.100, 11.200 and 11.300. It also omits the guidance's narrowed definition of a Part 11 record.

The guidance is nonbinding ('Contains Nonbinding Recommendations'). Enforcement discretion does not change the regulation's text, and predicate-rule requirements remain fully enforced. J says the latter but should label the guidance as nonbinding.
The question presupposes that Part 11 provisions apply to 'the vendor's controls'; the correct answer reframes this as the firm's responsibility for controls it relies on the vendor to implement.

explanation: 11.10 and 11.30 are the right regulatory anchors, and 11.3(b)(4)/(9) decides which one applies. J's description of the 2003 guidance (narrow scope, enforcement discretion, predicate rules still enforced) is broadly right but drops record retention from the discretion list. It does not say that FDA continues to enforce the remaining 11.10 controls and the signature provisions. It also never answers who bears the Part 11 obligation for vendor-operated controls. The guidance text could only be read via WebFetch, so confidence is Medium.
proposed_corrected_answer: Part 11 binds the regulated firm (the persons who use the system to create, modify, maintain or transmit the records), not the cloud vendor. The firm remains responsible for ensuring that controls implemented by the vendor meet Part 11 and the predicate rules. Whether 11.10 (closed system) or 11.30 (open system: 11.10 controls as appropriate plus measures such as encryption and digital signature standards) applies depends on whether system access is controlled by the persons responsible for the record content (11.3(b)(4), (b)(9)). If the LIMS uses electronic signatures, 11.50, 11.70, 11.100, 11.200 and 11.300 also apply. FDA's nonbinding 2003 guidance 'Part 11, Electronic Records; Electronic Signatures — Scope and Application' interprets Part 11 scope narrowly. Part 11 records are predicate-rule records maintained electronically in place of paper, or maintained electronically in addition to paper and relied on to perform regulated activities. FDA states it will exercise enforcement discretion for the validation, audit trail, record retention and record copying requirements (applying a justified, documented, risk-based approach) and for all Part 11 requirements for qualifying legacy systems (operational before Aug 20, 1997). FDA continues to enforce all other Part 11 provisions (e.g., 11.10(d), (f)-(k); 11.30; signature requirements) and all predicate-rule requirements, including record and recordkeeping requirements.

question_interpretation: Asks what the FSVP hazard analysis must cover.

issues.detail: J omits the requirement that the hazard analysis be written regardless of outcome (1.504(a)), the hazard types and sources that must be considered (biological, chemical incl. radiological, physical; natural, unintentional, or intentionally introduced for economic gain — 1.504(b)), and the probability/severity and factor-based evaluation (1.504(c)).

J omits 1.504(e) (biological hazards in covered produce need not be analyzed because they require a control) and 1.504(f) (no hazards requiring a control → no 1.505 evaluation or 1.506 verification, except for covered produce). It also omits that reliance on another entity requires documenting that a qualified individual did the analysis (1.504(d)).

explanation: 1.504 is the correct section and J's three elements are supported. But the written-analysis requirement is a core obligation, and the produce and no-hazard consequences are material. J's skeletal list would credit an answer that misses them.
proposed_corrected_answer: The importer must conduct a written hazard analysis (written regardless of outcome) for each type of food imported, identifying and evaluating known or reasonably foreseeable hazards to determine whether any require a control. It must cover biological, chemical (incl. radiological, pesticide/drug residues, allergens, etc.) and physical hazards, whether naturally occurring, unintentionally introduced, or intentionally introduced for economic gain. It must evaluate the probability and severity of each hazard, considering the food's formulation, the supplier's establishment, raw materials, transportation, processing, packaging and labeling, storage and distribution, intended use, sanitation and other factors, and must evaluate environmental pathogens for exposed RTE foods. The importer may instead review and assess another entity's hazard analysis, documenting that review and that a qualified individual performed it. For covered produce, biological hazards are deemed to require a control. If no hazards require a control, 1.505 evaluation and 1.506 verification are not required (except for covered produce).

proposed_corrected_answer: The importer must establish and follow written procedures to import only from approved foreign suppliers (or temporarily from unapproved suppliers whose food is verified first), and adequate written verification procedures. issues.detail: J's 'English language' element is wrong. 1.510 does not require FSVP records to be in English; FDA can only require an English translation within a reasonable time on request (1.510(b)(1)).

'Availability for FDA inspection within 24 hours' conflates two rules. Records must be available promptly on request (1.510(b)(1)), and offsite storage is allowed only if records can be retrieved and provided onsite within 24 hours (1.510(b)(2)). FDA may also require records to be sent electronically on written request (1.510(b)(3)).

Retention is 2 years after records are created or obtained, but records of processes and procedures (including evaluations and determinations) must be kept 2 years after their use is discontinued (1.510(c)(2)). proposed_corrected_answer: FSVP records may be original records, true copies or electronic records. FSVP records must be signed and dated on initial completion and on any modification, and must be legible and stored to prevent deterioration or loss. All records must be made available promptly to an authorized FDA representative on request for inspection and copying. Records may be in any language, but an English translation must be provided within a reasonable time on FDA request. Offsite storage (including records held by other entities) is permitted if records can be retrieved and provided onsite within 24 hours; electronic records accessible onsite count as onsite. On written FDA request, records must be sent electronically or by other prompt means. Retention is at least 2 years after records are created or obtained. Records of processes and procedures, including evaluations and determinations, must be kept for at least 2 years after their use is discontinued. FSVP-only electronic records are exempt from Part 11. issues.detail: J requires 'who must submit', but G omits 1.278. Under 1.278, any person with knowledge of the required information may submit (the submitter) and may use a transmitter. Any person with knowledge of the required information may submit it, alone or through a transmitter (1.278). It must be submitted electronically, in English with Latin characters, via ABI/ACE/ITDS or FDA PNSI (1.280), and FDA must confirm it no less than 2 hours before arrival by road, 4 hours by rail, 4 hours by air, and 8 hours by water. question_interpretation: Asks which foods are subject to the Subpart S additional traceability records and what must be recorded.

issues.detail: 'What must be recorded' is governed by 1.1325–1.1350, the key data elements for each critical tracking event (harvesting/cooling, initial packing, first land-based receiving, shipping, receiving, transformation), and by 1.1320 (when traceability lot codes are assigned). J omits the 1.1305 exemptions (e.g., small produce farms, certain small producers, foods receiving a kill step, retail/restaurants below thresholds) and that the FTL includes foods containing a listed food as an ingredient in the same form (1.1310 definition).

The rule is codified and current, but the original January 20, 2026 compliance date did not take effect for enforcement. FDA proposed extending it to July 20, 2028 (90 FR 38084), and Pub. L. 119-37 directed FDA not to enforce the rule before July 20, 2028 (91 FR 64656, Oct. 9, 2026). An answer should note this.

explanation: J's elements (FTL foods; CTEs and KDEs; traceability lot codes) are correct, and 1.1300/1.1310 support the 'which foods' part. But the provisions that say what must be recorded (1.1325–1.1350) and when TLCs are assigned (1.1320) are missing from G. 1.1315 concerns the traceability plan, not CTE records. A correct answer would cite sections the key omits.
proposed_corrected_answer: Subpart S applies to persons who manufacture, process, pack or hold foods on FDA's Food Traceability List (FTL), including foods that contain a listed food as an ingredient in the same form, subject to the 1.1305 exemptions. Covered persons must keep a traceability plan (1.1315). They must assign traceability lot codes at initial packing of RACs, first land-based receiving of seafood, and transformation, and must not assign new codes at other events (1.1320). They must keep records of key data elements linked to the traceability lot code for each critical tracking event: harvesting and cooling (1.1325), initial packing (1.1330), first land-based receiving (1.1335), shipping (1.1340), receiving (1.1345) and transformation (1.1350). These include the TLC, quantity and unit of measure, product description, location descriptions of the source, recipient and TLC source (or a TLC source reference), dates, and reference document type and number. Records are kept 2 years and provided to FDA within 24 hours, as an electronic sortable spreadsheet in outbreak situations (1.1455). FDA will not enforce the rule before July 20, 2028 under the Congressional directive in Pub. L. 119-37.

question_interpretation: Asks what a Subpart S traceability plan must contain and how long traceability records must be retained.

issues.detail: The question asks 'how long', but J says only 'record retention' without the period. Records must be kept 2 years from creation or receipt (1.1455(d)), and the previous traceability plan for 2 years after an update (1.1315(b)).

J omits the plan elements: a statement identifying a point of contact (1.1315(a)(4)), the procedures for identifying FTL foods (1.1315(a)(2)), the format and location of records (1.1315(a)(1)), and the duty to update the plan (1.1315(b)). The farm map applies only to growers or raisers of FTL foods other than eggs and must include geographic coordinates (aquaculture: containers).

Availability means within 24 hours of request (or a reasonable time FDA agrees to), with information needed to understand the records. An electronic sortable spreadsheet is required in outbreak, recall or threat situations unless the entity is below a size threshold (1.1455(c)). J's 'availability to FDA' gives no time limit.
FDA will not enforce Subpart S before July 20, 2028 (Pub. L. 119-37; 91 FR 64656).

explanation: G is correct: 1.1315 governs the plan and 1.1455 governs retention and availability. J's listed plan elements are supported. But J does not give the retention period the question asks for, omits the required point of contact, and gives no 24-hour availability standard.
proposed_corrected_answer: The traceability plan must describe: the procedures used to maintain Subpart S records, including their format and location; the procedures used to identify FTL foods handled; and how traceability lot codes are assigned under 1.1320, if applicable. It must also include a statement identifying a point of contact and, for anyone who grows or raises an FTL food other than eggs, a farm map showing each field or growing area (or aquaculture container) with geographic coordinates (1.1315(a)). The plan must be updated as needed, and the previous plan retained for 2 years after an update (1.1315(b)). Traceability records must be kept as original, true copies or electronic records for 2 years from the date created or obtained (1.1455(d)). They must be made available to FDA within 24 hours of request, or a reasonable time FDA agrees to, with information needed to understand them. In outbreak, recall or public-health threat situations, information must be provided as an electronic sortable spreadsheet unless the entity is below the size thresholds. An English translation must be given on request, and offsite storage is allowed if records can be retrieved within 24 hours (1.1455(c)). FDA will not enforce the rule before July 20, 2028 under Pub. L. 119-37.
